sections.title: Problem & context
paragraphs: A LoRaWAN deployment has several distinct boundaries: radio, gateway forwarding, network services and application integration. This lab documents the steps needed to bring those pieces together.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: The guides cover SSH and Azure network rules, PostgreSQL, Redis, Mosquitto and ChirpStack services. Separate documents describe gateway setup, LMIC-based Arduino nodes and local deployment options.

sections.title: Engineering decisions & challenges
paragraphs: Radio settings, device credentials and server connectivity must agree across independently configured components. The documentation breaks the work into server, gateway and node stages, with configuration examples and troubleshooting notes.

sections.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: The repository contains the deployment guides and gateway/device screenshots. It provides evidence of documented integration work, without establishing a production service or an independently repeated end-to-end acceptance test.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps
paragraphs: Azure IoT Hub, AWS IoT Core and application dashboards are roadmap ideas, not verified integrations. No range, availability or power-consumption result is asserted.

sections.title: Problem & context

sections.title: Implementation

sections.title: Engineering decisions & challenges

sections.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: The repository contains commands, explanations and real terminal/build screenshots across the five tasks. These are documented learning exercises, with no claimed production board-support package or measured target performance.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps

title: STM32 · SIM808 driver
summary: STM32 HAL C library defines SIM808 initialization, byte-wise UART receive interrupts and HTTP GET/POST routines.
notes: GET accepts a URL but does not configure it in the inspected function. Fixed delays, a hard-coded APN and an unbounded receive wait require hardening. The repository lacks the full generated STM32 project; do not claim standalone build success or dependable network handling.

media.alt: Conceptual illustration for STM32 · SIM808 driver, showing its engineering theme in cyan and violet field paths.
media.caption: Original conceptual illustration for this case study; it does not depict tested hardware, a real interface or measured results.

sections.title: Problem & context
paragraphs: Embedded applications often need a small communications layer between application code and a modem’s AT-command interface. This library explores that boundary with STM32 HAL and a SIM808 module.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: gprs_lib.c and its header define initialization, receive handling and GET/POST routines. main.c illustrates the integration surface. Incoming UART bytes feed a receive buffer while command helpers sequence modem operations.

sections.title: Engineering decisions & challenges
paragraphs: Serial commands and asynchronous responses need reliable coordination. The implementation uses interrupt-driven receive collection alongside fixed delays and receive waiting. That is a concrete starting point, but response parsing and timeout handling still require hardening.

sections.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: GET and POST function implementations and the receive callback are present. The source is a driver prototype, not a verified standalone firmware distribution; the complete generated STM32 project is not included.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps
paragraphs: The inspected GET function accepts a URL argument without configuring it. A fixed APN, fixed delays and an unbounded receive wait limit portability and resilience. No modem/network test was rerun for this portfolio.

sections.title: Problem & context
paragraphs: This academic SoPC project connects a processor implemented in programmable logic to physical input and output. The application changes a running LED sequence in response to switch input.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: The VHDL top level instantiates the generated system and connects I/O. The C application counts enabled switches and uses that count in its delay calculation while advancing an eight-LED pattern.

sections.title: Engineering decisions & challenges
paragraphs: Hardware port names and software peripheral addresses must agree. The Qsys design, top-level integration and PIO access make this hardware/software boundary explicit. Busy-wait timing remains a limitation rather than a calibrated timer.

sections.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: The checked C and VHDL implement the core switch-to-sequence behavior. The README provides a system screenshot and demonstration link. No hardware timing measurement was repeated for this portfolio.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps
paragraphs: The README leaves the board name as a placeholder and some file paths differ from the current tree. The case study does not infer a board model or precise timing.

sections.title: Problem & context
paragraphs: The project explores how a room-access system can connect on-device recognition with a reviewable record of access attempts. The CV and README describe a broader RFID, PIN and presence-sensing design; the public code supports a narrower, demonstrable image-and-event path.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: The capture script combines Picamera2, OpenCV and face_recognition, then posts events and image data to the server. Separate crypto helpers implement AES-CCM encryption and decryption. The web application separates monitoring routes, templates and stored event data.

sections.title: Engineering decisions & challenges
paragraphs: The design has to connect recognition, transport and image storage without treating them as a single opaque step. Separate capture, cryptographic and web components make these boundaries visible. The checked capture path generates RFID-like identifiers; a complete physical multi-factor validation sequence is not established by that script.

sections.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: Source inspection supports the recognition-to-dashboard path and encrypted-image helpers. The repository includes demonstration media and expected test scenarios. No independent accuracy, latency or security result is claimed.

sections.title: Limitations & next steps
paragraphs: The public capture path does not verify the full RFID/PIN flow described in the broader design. Key provisioning and secure transport need review before real deployment. A prototype is not a security assurance.
